text:
●​ No resume alone is going to get you a job. A successful job hunt is equal parts of five
     things–exploration, research, positioning, networking, and job hunt
         ○​ You have to explore the industry/role you specifically want, research the
            company you want, position yourself accordingly, network to get an inside
            referral, and then submit your resume.
                ■​ Recruiters love referrals because data shows that referred candidates get
                    hired faster and stay longer
  ●​ The average recruiter is juggling 30-40 open roles and the average job listing attracts
     250 resumes. The best recruiters used Linkedin, and they search by job title

●​ Alumni tool
         ○​ Navigating: Search school name in search bar > Click on school > Click on
            “Alumni” tab on home page
         ○​ Filtering: Search alumni by desired function (e.g. “product manager”, be sure to
            use quotes). You can continue to filter by company
         ○​ Connecting: If you find someone with whom you want to connect and message,
            without using premium, select “Connect” button > Add personalized message
  ●​ Linkedin cold outreach message guidelines (Commonality, Curiosity, and Call-to-Action)
         ○​ Sentence #1: Prove you’re not a stranger, state what you have in common: “I’m a
            current/alumni of (school), and I was thrilled to come across your profile.”
         ○​ Sentence #2: State what you are looking for–learning, a referral, a job, etc: “I’m
            torn between a PM and consulting career path and would love to learn from your
            expertise.”
○​ Sentence #3: Take all the friction out of the process: “Any chance you have 10
            minutes for a quick Zoom chat?”

●​ Linkedin recruiter gives people access to half a billion professionals globally. The tool is
     most geared towards 1) number of instances of key words (e.g. “brand marketing,”
     “product marketing,” etc.) 2) closeness of connection, and 3) photo
  ●​ Most important key word is the job title itself; most important placement: 1) Headline 2)
     Summary/About 3) Experience
         ○​ The algorithm places a high value on words in these three categories because
            they are the sections with the smallest character limit, placing greater value on
            the words within them
         ○​ Headline: “Aspiring Product Manager” or “Seeking Product Manager Roles”

○​ About: Include one line about what you are (e.g. “Experienced marketer with a
               track record of successful X: (list bullet points proving it)”) and include one line
               about what you want “Looking for a product manager? Contact me at (email)”
            ○​ Experience: Include resume points beneath each job
            ○​ Skills: Add and max out
  ●​   To identify key words needed, look at dream job postings and see what key words they
       use. This is what the recruiter and algorithm is using
            ○​ Use Jobscan and paste a copy of your profile versus a couple of your ideal job
               postings. This will give what % of the key words in the job description are
               reflected on your Linkedin profile and which ones to add
  ●​   Photo: Smiling and attire should match desired corporate culture (startup as casual,
       finance as formal, etc)

●​   Endorsements don’t show up on Linkedin recruiter. Recommendations appear in full on
       Linkedin recruiter. Go for quality over quantity (managers and clients, not subordinates)
       and ask them to include keywords
  ●​   If you want example profiles that worked, search “[School name] [Desired job title]” in the
       search bar, and find people’s profile who are in the position you want to be in. Emulate
       what they have done
  ●​   Cover photo: Go to Pexels and search for royalty-free images
  ●​   Follow the companies where you want to work

●​ If you have a job you really want, see who posted the role, and connect with that
     recruiter. If you don’t get it, you can always follow-up with the recruiter after the fact
  ●​ Create alerts for jobs that meet desired criteria. The alert will only show you the new jobs
     posted that meet your criteria, not all thousands of roles
          ○​ Navigation: Search for jobs > Click “create alert” > Set frequency
          ○​ You can also set an alert for one company at a time, to show you what kinds of
             new jobs they are posting, where are they growing and see the biggest need
  ●​ Toggle “Open to opportunities” button to be seen by recruiters. This can be a first filter for
     the recruiter to test whether their applicant pool will respond

○​ It is by default turned off that your current company can see whether or not you
             turn it on
  ●​ When searching for roles via the search bar, use the filters to narrow down thousands of
     results
          ○​ Time frame: Start by filtering those that were posted in the past week
          ○​ Experience level: Include “safety” and “stretch” seniority
          ○​ Company: Filter by desired size
          ○​ On-side/remote, full-time/part-time, etc.
  ●​ When you find a posting you like, click on it (every posting is hyperlinked) to see the full
     posting > Scroll down > See “Similar jobs” section. This can help broaden list of potential
     employers
  ●​ To automatically share your profile with a recruiter, go to Settings > Data Privacy > Job
     Seeking Preferences > “Share your profile when you click Apply for a job” > On

●​ To signal to a particular company that you want to work for them, and that you’re
     interested in them specifically, go to go to Settings > Data Privacy > Job Seeking
     Preferences > Share job alerts and signal interest to recruiters > “On”

●​ Second degree connections
        ○​ Search “[Name of company] [Role]” in search bar and look for those that have a
           shared connection (2nd degree connection) > Select 2nd degree connection >
           Click name of mutual connection > Send message to mutual connectino
        ○​ For example, if you want to reach out to John Doe on Google’s Product
           Marketing team, and you have a mutual connection Jane, reach out to Jane via
           messaging with the following
               ■​ “Hi Jane, Would you mind introducing me to John? I’m thinking about
                  applying for jobs in his field but want to make sure it is a good fit. If you’re
                  willing to do so, I’ve included a message below that you can just forward
                  over

<<<Message to Forward>>>
                     Hi John,
                     I recently came across your profile on LinkedIn and was so fascinated by
                     all the awesome things you’ve done. In particular, I’d love to learn about
                     your experience with product marketing, as I’m considering that field
                     myself.
                     That said, I know you must be incredibly busy right now. But if you have
                     even 10 minutes to chat in the next few weeks, just let me know as I’d
                     love to learn from your expertise!
                     Thanks for considering!
  ●​ Alumni connections
        ○​ Search “[Name of company] [Role]” in search bar > All filters tab in upper
            righthand corner > Click “Add School” under the school section and type in your
            college > Click show results > Select a person to whom you can connect and
            “Add note” to connection request​
                ■​ If you reach your personalized note limits, here is workaround

○​ Example outreach message “I came across your profile and, as a fellow [College]
            grad. I’d be thrilled to learn about your experience with [Role.] Any chance you
            have 10 minutes to chat next week? I'd love to get your advice!
  ●​ Networking question ideas
        ○​ It's great to connect with you via [Name] - thanks for making the time!

○​ I'd love to learn about your experience at [Company]. What led you to work
            there?
         ○​ What's kept you there over time?
         ○​ What's it like on the inside - and specifically as a [role]?

●​ Read through a company’s page. Use their same language in your interview and/or
     resume
  ●​ To find big voices by function or company, search key words in the search bar > Select
     “Posts” and Linkedin will show the posts where the keyword appears that are the most
     popular. This can highlight big names, or at least well-followed, in the space
         ○​ Follow a few of the “Linkedin influencers” to see what is happening in the industry
             and learn the language
  ●​ Follow the same process for groups as you do for big voices
         ○​ You can join groups on function or role and message people within that group
             who share similar characteristics (school, etc)
  ●​ To anticipate potential interview questions, click the Job icon > Interview prep to see
     common practice questions
         ○​ Click “Categories” to narrow down further

●​ Most unfiltered feedback will come from people who used to work at the company
         ○​ All People > Advanced search > Past company [Name of company]
         ○​ Example message: “Just saw that you used to work at [Company] and was quite
             intrigued. Especially since I'm considering an offer there right now. Might you
             have 15 minutes to chat this week about your experience?"
         ○​ Ask them these two essential questions:
                  ■​ Why did you leave?
                  ■​ Would you ever work there again?
  ●​ The most useful data point in salary negotiations is how much the competition is paying

section: Session #3 - Reading Job Descriptions for Resume Edits
text:
●​ Look for repeated words in a target job description and try to repeat those in your
     resume bullets
          ○​ “Creativity” = highlight thinking outside the box
          ○​ “Monetization” = what did you monetize
          ○​ “Cross-functional leadership” = working with multiple teams simultaneously
          ○​ Particularly, if they tell you who their customers are, and you have experience
             working with these stakeholders, highlight this
  ●​ If the posting says “The successful candidate must commit to XYZ dates,” be ready to
     commit to these. Don’t ask for an exception
  ●​ Really long phrases (bullets that are extra long or at a greater level of detail than the
     others) suggest this is a pain point in the company; network to confirm this is the case
     and emphasize the skills that can “fix” or combat this
  ●​ Most job descriptions are templates that hiring managers then tweak for the most
important aspects of the role. If there is a phrase that is a-typical, it means it was
     intentionally changed
  ●​ Networking question idea: What are the traits of the most successful person?

●​ Formatting varies for the intended next move. The goal is readability because recruiters
     spend 7-8 seconds per resume, so your goal is marketing
          ○​ Chronological: 1) “Classic/traditional” industries like banking, consulting, etc. 2)
             Single pivot (same role, new industry or new industry, same role)
          ○​ Hybrid:
                 ■​ Definition: Job titles all in a row under the company name. Then sections
                     of bullets fall under function or skill–“Cross-functional leadership,”
                     "Analytical problem solving,” “Organizational strategy and influence,” etc.
                 ■​ Ensure your categories are your strengths
          ○​ Functional (most rate): 1) Big pivots 2) Unfamiliar industries (e.g. teaching) 3)
             Transferable skills 4) Whole career has been in one industry and jobs are so
             similar
  ●​ If you are pivoting, the first question you will get in an interview is why the change. If
     there is doubt about your skills, network to have an internal advocate convince internally
that you can do the role
  ●​ If you worked at a niche company (or one that would not be widely known) pick attributes
     that would be appealing to your target audience–revenue, number of countries,

examples of customers/big brands, “the biggest [industry] company and first tech
       unicorn”
  ●​   There are attributes you can use to connect with new companies when making a
       pivot–rapid growth in your resume, similar customer bases (size, region, industry), B2B
       vs B2C
  ●​   Applicant tracking system (ATS)
           ○​ ATS systems neither accept nor reject your resume; it indexes them to make it
              easier for the recruiter to read your resume. Haas’ standard format makes this
              easier by design
           ○​ Recruiters don’t put any value in algorithm-generated resume “rating.” They rely
              on 8-second personal, “human” scan
  ●​   Remove undergrad GPA because the moment it’s added it opens you up to comparison
  ●​   Remove undergrad awards unless you have space
  ●​   Make sure you have an additional section and be humorous to entice the reader to ask
       you about it. The section should be 1-3 lines
○​ Example: Interests: Amateur backyard farmer, optimistic AI futurist, and
              washed-up distance runner (former D1 athlete.)

●​ Resume bullets should include 3/4 elements at a minimum
        ○​ What: The thing, or “work object,” you made

○​ How: What skills you used to make that work object (skills should be tailored to
              the employer/role)
          ○​ Impact: Measurable outcome ideally
          ○​ Why: Why was it important, was it part of a company’s bigger strategy? How
              often did you do it, etc.
●​   Start with “impact” if it is large; start with “how” if you are pivoting industry, or potentially
     role, where the vocabulary is not the same
●​   All bullets should be explicit rather than intentionally mysterious to generate curiosity or a
     follow-up question
●​   Adjectives and adverbs is what makes a bullet long
●​   Use abbreviations only if you are moving within the same industry or function
●​   Gen AI use cases
          ○​ Rewrite your bullets
          ○​ Point out what’s moving
          ○​ Improve readability
●​   Gen AI quality controls–is everything true, check for too much jargon (including
adjectives and adverbs), 3-letter acronyms, read it outloud, and ensure the bullets
     include the three elements (what, how, why)
●​   If you don’t know what the impact for a bullet is (this happens often in consulting), put
     down what the projected impact would be

●​ Six steps of a successful job search
         ○​ 0) Clarity on your “way” and your interests
         ○​ 1) Desk research
                  ■​ This can be 20 minutes. It does not have to be exhaustive
         ○​ 2) Value proposition development
                  ■​ This combines desk research and how you can help. You position
                      yourself as being able to contribute to an initiative or solve a problem.
                      What do you bring to the table that is interesting to that company?
         ○​ 3) Low-to-medium stakes pressure test and feedback
                  ■​ Low-stakes: CMG, Haas undergrad (first-years, second-years, and
                      EWMBA), peer advisors, faculty
                  ■​ Medium-stakes: Case competition, Haas networking events, alumni
         ○​ 4) Revise and refine
         ○​ 5) High stakes pressure test and feedback
                  ■​ High stakes: Application or interview
                  ■​ Long before you get to this stage, you should iterate earlier; learn what
                      questions or challenges to anticipate, gaps in your company knowledge,
                      etc.

■​ Feedback in high stakes testing can be limited; whether you are declined,
                      and at what stage, is feedback
         ○​ 6) Revise and refine
  ●​ As you move down the funnel your personal value prop and target network gets more
     specific
  ●​ Most common step missed is step #1; if you skip it, every subsequent step in the
     process suffers
  ●​ Desk research
         ○​ Your why: Personal and resonates with you
         ○​ Interests and preferences: Interesting or matters to you (e.g. sector, company
              size geography, roles, functions, remove/hybrids, values)
         ○​ Domain knowledge interests: Specific (beyond popular knowledge) and
              interesting to you, strategic/operational priorities/challenges of the organization
         ○​ Resources for desk research: WSJ, Forbes, annual reports (especially
              footnotes,) financial times, Youtube, listen to quarterly earnings review with the
              analysts (particularly the questions to understand where they are growing)
  ●​ Developing value proposition

○​ Resume, refining response to “tell me about yourself,” transferable skills, and
              career conversations (networking)
                  ■​ Career conversations comes down to the quality of questions that you
                      ask, which is dependent on your desk research
  ●​ Prioritizing: Making consistent choices that advance you towards your highest goal
         ○​ You have 18 hours per week to manage, and in order to prioritize you have to
              make hard decisions that makes someone (including yourself) unhappy

■​ You sometimes have to “disappoint” yourself in order to achieve your
                  long-term goals
  ●​ Do what you need to do, not what others can afford to do

●​ Recommended read: The Two Hour Job Search
  ●​ Process for networking:
          ○​ 1) Generate a hypothesis to explore–industry, function, location, etc.
          ○​ 2) Generate learning targets–40-50 target companies and look at their earnings,
             strategy, etc.
          ○​ 3) Begin your networking list–people from undergrad and grad who work there
          ○​ 4) Plan first outreach
  ●​ Benefits of networking–refine target industry and roles, learn the vocabulary, identify
     hidden opportunities (60% of jobs are not posted,) practice and refine your personal
     pitch, and build relationships
          ○​ The further you are in your career, or after your MBA graduation date, the more
             likely your next job is going to come from your network
  ●​ Referrals
          ○​ Referrals come after you build the trusting relationship; start with a networking
             call, keep in touch with them, and then ask for the referral; never ask for a referral
             in the first call

○​ Getting a referral from someone in another city/office can be valuable, but its
             depends on the company, city, culture, etc
          ○​ Wait until after the first conversation to ask who else to whom else to talk; the first
             networking call is all about the other person–your curiosity in what they do or how
             they do it
  ●​ Exploratory conversations
          ○​ Start networking only but only after desk research about the person, company,
             etc.
  ●​ Developing company and industry focus list
          ○​ If you say “tech,” what type of tech? If you say “fintech” what type of fintech?
             Start with dream employers
          ○​ If you aren't sure where to start for your target list of companies, look at
             conferences of interest and make a list of companies attending and sponsors
          ○​ The CMG (Haas Career Management Group) has seen success with student

cold-calling dream companies. It requires more desk work and more guts
  ●​ If you are apprehensive about not being “ready” before an exploratory conversation, be
     upfront about this and impress them with your preparation and questions. Don’t let the
     feeling of “not be ready” prevent you from having a call
  ●​ Outreach principles
          ○​ 1) Short (<100 words)
                  ■​ Only ask for 15-20 minutes
          ○​ 2) No mention of you looking for or asking for jobs/internships

○​ 3) State your connection up front
               ■​ “Ex-Fintech to Fintech” or “From Haasie to Haasie” subject line
       ○​ 4) Generalize interest in industry/role
       ○​ 5) It’s about them
●​ Follow-up
       ○​ 1) Thank you note
       ○​ 2) Keep them in the loop, or the “post card” strategy–where you traveled to and
          that you’re thinking of them
               ■​ Another way to keep in touch is notifying them of milestones–finishing the
                   semester, coming back from a trip, etc. For example, “I just came back
                   from winter break. I’ve talked to more companies and remain really
                   interested. I found XYZ interesting. If more happens, I’ll let you know. Let
                   me know if you’re in the area, and it would be great to meet for coffee”
●​ Goal: 2 outreaches per week

- The About section should include a summary of your experience and what you are looking for. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*
- Use Jobscan to check the percentage of keywords from job descriptions reflected in your profile. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*

- Create job alerts to receive notifications for new roles matching desired criteria. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*
- Use filters to narrow results by time frame (e.g., past week), experience level, company size, and work type. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*
- Toggle the 'Open to opportunities' button to be visible to recruiters. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*
- Automatically share your profile when applying for a job is an option in settings. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*
- Signal interest to a company by sharing job alerts and signaling interest to recruiters. *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training .pdf|Aug 2025 - Linkedin Training]])*

This section outlines methods for researching companies and preparing for interviews using LinkedIn features. It suggests using company language and searching for popular posts and groups to find industry insights.

- Hybrid format places job titles all in a row under the company name with sections of bullets under function or skill *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training.pdf|Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training]])*
- Functional format is most rated for big pivots, unfamiliar industries, transferable skills, or when the whole career is in one industry *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training.pdf|Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training]])*
- Remove undergrad GPA because it opens you up to comparison *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training.pdf|Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training]])*
- Remove undergrad awards unless you have space *(source: [[raw/Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training.pdf|Aug 2025 - Resume & Networking Training]])*
